howto.name: How to check AI use in Medicare coverage decisions for compliance

steps.name: List every tool in the decision path
steps.text: Record each algorithm or AI system that touches a coverage, utilization or care decision for Medicare beneficiaries: what it predicts, what data it reads, and which decision it feeds.

steps.name: Prove the human decides
steps.text: For every adverse medical necessity decision, show that a physician or qualified professional reviewed the individual record, with the tool's output as one input, as 42 CFR 422.101(c) and 422.566(d) require.

steps.name: Publish and freeze the criteria
steps.text: Post the coverage criteria the tool applies where the public can read them, and show the tool cannot change them as it learns.

steps.name: Run the Section 1557 review
steps.text: Identify any decision support tool that uses race, color, national origin, sex, age or disability as an input, and document the mitigation, as 45 CFR 92.210 requires.

steps.name: Measure the clocks
steps.text: Report standard and expedited decision times against the CMS limits, and the share of denials overturned on appeal, because a high overturn rate is the first thing a regulator reads as a tool doing the deciding.

short: How AI is used in Medicare Advantage and Original Medicare coverage decisions, the CMS and HHS rules that limit it, and what a beneficiary can do about an AI-assisted denial.
title: Medicare and AI
subtitle: Coverage decisions, prior authorization and a beneficiary's rights
body_html:
On this page

  • Who this page is for
  • Where AI touches Medicare today
  • The rules that apply
  • WISeR: AI prior authorization in Original Medicare
  • What a beneficiary can do
  • What plans, vendors and providers must show
  • Sources

Who this page is for

Two readers. A person on Medicare who wants to know whether a computer is deciding what their plan will pay for, and what they can do about it. And a plan, a vendor or a provider that uses artificial intelligence in Medicare work and needs to know which rules already reach it. The short answer for both: AI may assist a Medicare coverage decision, but under current federal rules it may not be the decision, and the person affected keeps every appeal right they had before.

Where AI touches Medicare today

Medicare Advantage prior authorization. Private Medicare Advantage plans use software, including AI, to help decide whether a service is medically necessary before they pay for it. This is where most beneficiary complaints arise, and it is the reason CMS wrote the rules described below. A 2022 review by the HHS Office of Inspector General found that 13 percent of the prior authorization requests Medicare Advantage plans denied actually met Medicare coverage rules.

Original Medicare, in six states. Traditional Medicare historically required almost no prior authorization. That changed on January 1, 2026, when the CMS Innovation Center began the WISeR model, which uses AI and machine learning contractors to review a short list of services in Arizona, New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, Texas and Washington. Details are in the WISeR section.

CMS operations. CMS itself uses AI to find billing anomalies, flag likely fraud and manage claims and enrollment data, under a published CMS AI Playbook at ai.cms.gov. This affects providers far more than beneficiaries.

Consumer tools. Plan comparison sites, insurer apps and general chatbots use AI to explain Medicare terms and enrollment windows. None of them can reliably confirm whether a specific doctor is in a specific plan's network, whether a specific drug is on a formulary, or what an individual will owe. Those answers still come from Medicare.gov, the plan, or a State Health Insurance Assistance Program counselor.

The rules that apply

Medicare Advantage must decide on the individual, not the average. CMS's contract year 2024 Medicare Advantage rule (CMS-4201-F) requires plans to base medical necessity decisions on the circumstances of the specific patient, under 42 CFR 422.101(c). In a February 6, 2024 memo answering questions on that rule, CMS said an algorithm or AI tool may assist a coverage decision, but a tool that determines coverage from a larger data set instead of the individual patient's medical history, the physician's recommendations, or clinical notes does not comply. CMS gave the example of post-acute care: software may predict a likely length of stay, but that prediction alone cannot be the basis for ending coverage; the patient's own condition must be reassessed first.

An adverse decision needs a qualified human. Under 42 CFR 422.566(d), a Medicare Advantage denial on medical necessity grounds must be reviewed by a physician or other appropriate health professional with expertise in the relevant field. An AI output is not that review.

Coverage criteria must be public and must not drift. Where Medicare's own coverage rules are fully established, a plan may not deny on stricter internal criteria. Where a plan uses internal criteria, they must be based on current clinical evidence and published where the public can read them (42 CFR 422.101(b)(6)). CMS's memo adds that an algorithm may not shift those criteria over time as it takes in more data.

Prior authorization has clocks. Standard requests must be decided within 14 days and expedited requests within 72 hours; under the interoperability and prior authorization rule (CMS-0057-F) the standard window shortens to 7 days for Medicare Advantage beginning in 2026. An approval must be honored for the course of treatment, and a plan may not impose a new prior authorization on a new enrollee in an active course of treatment for 90 days.

No discrimination through the tool. The Section 1557 rule HHS finalized in May 2024 added 45 CFR 92.210, which took effect May 1, 2025. Covered health programs, including Medicare Advantage plans and providers that take Medicare, must make reasonable efforts to identify patient care decision support tools that use race, color, national origin, sex, age or disability as an input, and must mitigate the risk of discrimination from them. HHS's Office for Civil Rights enforces this; the site's HHS OCR AI enforcement page covers how.

Privacy. Any AI that touches a beneficiary's health information is inside HIPAA: minimum necessary access, a business associate agreement with the vendor, audit logs, breach notification. The HIPAA and AI page has the detail.

WISeR: AI prior authorization in Original Medicare

The Wasteful and Inappropriate Service Reduction model is a six-year CMS Innovation Center test, January 1, 2026 through December 31, 2031, in six states: Arizona, New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, Texas and Washington. Contractors experienced in prior authorization, paid a share of the savings from requests that do not result in a paid claim, use AI and machine learning alongside clinical review to decide requests for a defined list of services CMS considers prone to waste or harm, such as skin and tissue substitutes, electrical nerve stimulators and epidural steroid injections. Requests began on January 5, 2026, for services on or after January 15, 2026.

What CMS has said does not change: Medicare coverage policy itself, so a covered service stays covered; the requirement that a denial be reviewed by a clinician; and providers' existing appeal rights. Decisions are expected within 72 hours, or 48 hours when expedited. CMS has said contractors are paid to get the determination right rather than to deny, and that a gold card exemption for providers with high approval rates is planned.

The model is contested. Members of Congress have argued it imports Medicare Advantage's prior authorization problems into traditional Medicare, and a bill introduced on December 2, 2025, the Ban AI Denials in Medicare Act (H.R. 6361), would prohibit it. As of this page's date the model is running.

What a beneficiary can do

If your Medicare Advantage plan denies a service. You may ask for a reconsideration within 65 days of the denial notice. The plan must decide a standard reconsideration within 30 days, or within 72 hours if your doctor says waiting could seriously harm you. If the plan upholds its denial, it must automatically send your case to an independent review entity; you do not have to ask. Ask your doctor to write a letter tying the request to your own history, because the rule the plan must follow is about your circumstances, not a statistical average.

If a claim is denied in Original Medicare. Your Medicare Summary Notice tells you how to ask for a redetermination, which you may request within 120 days. In the six WISeR states, a prior authorization denial can be resubmitted with more documentation and, if a claim is then denied, appealed the same way.

Ask whether software was used. A plan must give you the specific reason for a denial and the coverage criteria it applied. You are entitled to ask whether an algorithm or AI tool was involved and to insist the decision reflect your medical record.

Get free help. Every state has a State Health Insurance Assistance Program with trained counselors, reachable through Medicare.gov or 1-800-MEDICARE. Nothing on this page is legal or medical advice; for a decision about your own care, check the primary sources below and speak to your plan, your doctor or a counselor.

What plans, vendors and providers must show

The controls CMS and HHS expect follow from the rules above: a written record of every AI or algorithm used in coverage or care decisions and what it does; evidence that adverse decisions are made by a qualified clinician on the individual record, with the tool's output as one input; published coverage criteria that the tool cannot alter; a Section 1557 review of each decision support tool for protected inputs, with mitigation documented; HIPAA safeguards and business associate agreements for every vendor that touches beneficiary data; and reporting on decision times against the prior authorization clocks. For providers in the WISeR states, that means knowing which of your services are on the list and building the documentation the contractor's review will look for.

Sources

  • CMS, Frequently Asked Questions related to Coverage Criteria and Utilization Management Requirements in CMS Final Rule (CMS-4201-F), February 6, 2024.
  • CMS, Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule, CMS-0057-F, January 2024.
  • CMS Innovation Center, Wasteful and Inappropriate Service Reduction (WISeR) Model, announced June 27, 2025; Federal Register notice; Provider and Supplier Operational Guide.
  • HHS, Nondiscrimination in Health Programs and Activities, Section 1557 final rule, May 2024, 45 CFR 92.210.
  • HHS Office of Inspector General, Some Medicare Advantage Organization Denials of Prior Authorization Requests Raise Concerns, April 2022.
  • CMS, AI Playbook, ai.cms.gov.
  • H.R. 6361, Ban AI Denials in Medicare Act, introduced December 2, 2025.
